idiom_name: Spring Security authorizeHttpRequests ending in anyRequest().denyAll(); Jakarta @DenyAll / @RolesAllowed
implementation_notes: Java's authorization lives in frameworks rather than in the language: Spring Security's `AuthorizationFilter` evaluates `authorizeHttpRequests` rules in declaration order, and the reference documentation recommends ending the list with a rule that denies anything unmatched - 'Any URL that has not already been matched on is denied access. This is a good strategy if you do not want to accidentally forget to update your authorization rules.' By default Spring Security requires every request to be authenticated, and any `HttpSecurity` instance makes declaring the rules mandatory. The declarative complement is Jakarta Annotations: `@RolesAllowed` names the grants and `@DenyAll` marks methods that no role may invoke, enforced by the container instead of by application code. Either way the grant set is configuration - roles, authorities, policies - reviewable and versioned, and the default case (no matching rule, no annotation) is the denied one.
pitfalls: Leaving out the final catch-all: an unmatched request is not automatically denied by your rule list, and a broad `permitAll()` pattern (`/api/**`) reopens everything under it; end with `anyRequest().denyAll()` or a deliberate authenticated rule.

`AuthorizationFilter` runs on every dispatch (REQUEST, FORWARD, ERROR, INCLUDE), so error and forward dispatches are authorized too; a blanket permit for ERROR dispatches added to make error pages render can also permit access through forwarded paths - scope dispatcher rules narrowly.

Web rules and method security are separate layers: `@PreAuthorize`/`@RolesAllowed` on services are not applied by URL rules, and internal calls that never cross the proxy (self-invocation) skip the method check; the enforcement point must sit on the path actually taken.

Jakarta annotation defaults are container-specific: a method without an annotation is unchecked unless the class declares otherwise, so mark sensitive methods `@DenyAll`/`@RolesAllowed` explicitly rather than relying on absence.

The JVM's historic stack-walking default-deny (AccessController/SecurityManager) is deprecated for removal and disabled in later releases, with no replacement: new code must not be built on it - the framework or container is the enforcement point.
